value.overview: The Buff-rumped Warbler is a small, active New World warbler strongly associated with clear streams and other flowing water in tropical forests. Its most distinctive feature is the rich buff coloring on the rump and upper tail, which is especially noticeable when the bird flicks or fans its tail. Unlike many North American warblers, it is largely sedentary. In Costa Rica, it is a resident species of humid lowland and foothill habitats, where it is often found beside shaded forest streams.
value.classification: The Buff-rumped Warbler belongs to the family Parulidae and the genus Myiothlypis. Its scientific name is Myiothlypis fulvicauda; older literature may place it in Basileuterus or Phaeothlypis.
value.identification: This warbler is about 13–14 cm long. It has olive-brown upperparts, a grayish head, a pale buff or yellowish eyebrow, and yellowish underparts that may appear paler in some individuals. The bright buff rump and buff upper tail are its key field marks. The wings and central tail feathers are darker, while pale markings on the outer tail can be visible as it moves. It frequently pumps or flicks its tail while walking along stream margins.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from eastern and southern Mexico or Central America through Panama and much of northern and western South America, with a separate population in parts of the western Amazon Basin. In Costa Rica it occurs mainly in wet Caribbean-slope forests, humid foothills, and suitable sites on the southern Pacific slope. It favors shaded, fast-flowing streams, small rivers, ravines, and forest edges near water, generally from low elevations into the foothills and locally higher elevations. Dense ground vegetation and mossy banks are typical surroundings.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range; it does not undertake regular long-distance migration. Local movements may occur when birds follow suitable streamside habitat or seasonal changes in water conditions.
value.breeding: The Buff-rumped Warbler usually nests close to water. Its nest is a bulky, covered structure with a side entrance, commonly placed on or beside a sloping stream bank, path bank, or other sheltered ground location. The female typically lays about two white eggs. Incubation lasts roughly 16–17 days, and young leave the nest after approximately two weeks. In Costa Rica, breeding can occur within its year-round range, although the timing may vary with local rainfall and elevation.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet consists mainly of insects and other small invertebrates, including insect larvae and spiders. The bird forages on the ground and among rocks, leaf litter, moss, roots, and low vegetation beside streams. It may make short movements to seize prey from wet surfaces or shallow water margins. Its preference for running water and streamside cover distinguishes its feeding habitat from that of many other tropical warblers.
value.behavior: This is an energetic, often conspicuous streamside warbler. It walks and hops along rocks, muddy banks, and low vegetation, frequently flicking its tail and moving continuously while searching for prey. Pairs or individuals may defend territories along streams and give sharp calls or a ringing song from low perches. It is usually encountered alone or in pairs, although it can occasionally join mixed-species foraging groups in forested areas.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species is not currently assessed as undergoing a sufficiently rapid decline to qualify for a threatened category.
